title.en: Sign up for emergency alerts

description.en: Turn on Wireless Emergency Alerts on your phone (iPhone: Settings → Notifications → scroll to Government Alerts; Android: Settings → Notifications → Emergency Alerts). Then register for your county's local alert system.

title.en: Know your tsunami evacuation route

description.en: Walk or drive your route from home to the nearest tsunami safe zone in daylight, before you need it. Maps for every island are at the HI-EMA link below. If you live within a half mile of the coast, plan to evacuate on foot — roads jam in a warning.

title.en: Identify two evacuation routes

description.en: Your primary route may be blocked by debris, traffic, or downed lines. Walk both routes once so you know them by sight, not by phone.

sources.label: Red Cross — How to Prepare for Emergencies

title.en: Practice your evacuation plan with your household

description.en: Walk through it once with everyone who lives with you, including kids and elderly relatives. Decide where you'll meet if you get separated and how you'll find each other if cell service is down.

sources.label: Red Cross — Make a Family Emergency Plan

title.en: Build a grab-and-go bag

description.en: A small backpack near your door with: 1 day of water and food per person, copies of IDs, cash, medications for 3 days, a phone charger, a flashlight, and a change of clothes. Designed for evacuations where you have minutes, not hours.

title.en: Build a 14-day emergency kit

description.en: Hawaiʻi's official guidance is 14 days of supplies, not the mainland's 3 days, because of our isolation from supply chains. Cover water (1 gallon per person per day), shelf-stable food, medications, batteries, cash, important documents, and a first-aid kit.

title.en: Document your home for an insurance claim

description.en: Walk every room with your phone camera, recording video and photos. Open closets and drawers. Store the file in cloud storage. After a disaster you'll need to prove what you owned; memory and paperwork are not enough.

title.en: Learn how to host evacuating neighbors

description.en: If your home is above the evacuation zone, families fleeing the coast may walk to your neighborhood during a warning. Knowing a few neighbors, having an extra gallon of water, and leaving your porch light on at night is most of what it takes.

title.en: Review your flood insurance coverage

description.en: Standard homeowner's insurance does NOT cover flood damage. If you're in a FEMA flood zone, federally backed mortgages usually require flood insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program; otherwise it's optional but often a good idea. There's a 30-day waiting period after purchase before coverage starts — don't wait until a storm is forecast.

title.en: Create defensible space around your home

description.en: Clear dry brush, leaves, and dead vegetation within 30 feet of your house. Keep grass mowed short in dry months. Trim tree branches at least 10 feet from your roof and chimney. This is the single highest-impact thing you can do to reduce your home's wildfire risk.

sources.label: Hawaiʻi Wildfire Management Organization — Ready, Set, Go!

title.en: Harden your home against ember ignition

description.en: Most homes lost to wildfire ignite from windborne embers, not direct flame. Highest-leverage upgrades: install a Class-A fire-rated roof, screen all roof and foundation vents with 1/8-inch metal mesh, replace flammable mulch with gravel near the house, and remove anything wooden touching the exterior walls (woodpiles, dead plants, doormats).

actions.estimatedTime: varies — 2 hours to plan, days to execute

title.en: Evaluate flood-proofing options for your home

description.en: Talk to your county building department or a licensed contractor about whether your home's mechanical and electrical systems (water heater, washer, dryer, electrical panel) sit above the base flood elevation. Backflow valves on sewer connections, raised utilities, and graded landscaping can substantially reduce damage in a flood.

actions.estimatedTime: 1 hour to research, more to implement

title.en: Prepare for hurricane and coastal-storm conditions

description.en: In hurricane season (June–November), know which county hurricane refuge serves your area, plan how you would board windows or move outdoor objects indoors, and keep your vehicle fueled in the days a major storm is forecast. Hawaiʻi's last major direct strike was Iniki in 1992.

title.en: Subscribe to USGS volcano updates

description.en: The USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory posts daily and weekly updates on Kīlauea and Mauna Loa. Subscribe to email notifications so you hear about activity changes before you see them on the news. Follow Hawaiʻi County Civil Defense for evacuation guidance.

title.en: Make a household communication plan

description.en: Pick an out-of-state contact everyone in your household will call or text if local lines are jammed. Agree on two meeting places — one near home and one outside the neighborhood. Decide who picks up kids from school, and what happens if you're at work and can't reach home.

title.en: Prepare an evacuation document folder

description.en: Scan and store in cloud storage: photo IDs and passports, insurance policies, mortgage or rental agreement, medical records and prescriptions, and recent photos of your home. Print one paper copy and keep it with your grab-and-go bag. You'll be glad you did when rebuilding after a major event.

title.en: Add infant supplies to your emergency kit

description.en: Pack a sealed bag with at least two weeks of formula or food, a clean bottle, diapers and wipes for two weeks, infant medications you can't get same-day, a change of clothes for several sizes ahead, and a copy of your pediatrician's contact info. Rotate the food and check fit every few months.

sources.label: Red Cross — Disaster Supplies for Infants

title.en: Build a pet evacuation kit

description.en: Pack a carrier or leash, two weeks of food and water, your pet's medications, a recent photo of you with your pet (in case you get separated), and copies of vaccination records. Hawaiʻi shelters do not all accept pets — call ahead or check your county's list of pet-friendly shelters now.

title.en: Register with your county for medical-needs assistance

description.en: If a household member depends on electricity for medical equipment, contact your county civil defense to ask about a special-needs registry. Where one exists, registering means first responders know to check on you during outages and evacuations. If your county doesn't keep a registry, ask which programs do (power-utility medical baseline lists, neighborhood watch, kūpuna programs).

title.en: Register with your county for evacuation assistance

description.en: If a household member uses a wheelchair, walking aid, or otherwise needs help evacuating, contact your county civil defense to ask about a special-needs registry. Where one exists, registering means first responders know to check on you and what kind of help you'll need.

title.en: Plan a backup power source for medical equipment

description.en: Decide now what you'll do if the power is out for days. Options: a portable battery sized for your equipment, a small generator with safe outdoor placement, an arrangement with a friend or shelter that has power, or notifying your utility company in advance that you're on a medical-baseline list. Don't wait for a forecast — talk to your equipment supplier this month.

actions.estimatedTime: 1 hour to plan, more to implement

title.en: Identify an accessibility-compatible shelter near you

description.en: Not all evacuation shelters are equipped for wheelchairs, walking aids, or medical equipment. Call your county civil defense to ask which nearby shelters are accessibility-compatible, and write the answer down where you can find it during an evacuation.

sources.label: Red Cross — People with Disabilities and Disasters

title.en: Plan an evacuation route that doesn't require a car

description.en: If you can't drive yourself out, decide now who picks you up or how you'll evacuate on foot. Ask a neighbor who drives; identify the closest bus route; print a walking map to your nearest safe zone. In a no-notice event (local tsunami, fast wildfire), walking on foot to higher ground or away from the coast may be the only option.

title.en: Confirm your landlord's emergency contact and inspection schedule

description.en: As a renter, your landlord is responsible for the building's structural integrity, but you may not know how they handle disaster damage or inspections. Get a working emergency phone number, ask whether the building has a posted evacuation plan, and confirm whether your renter's insurance covers your possessions in a flood, fire, or earthquake.

title.en: Know your building's evacuation plan

description.en: If you live in an apartment, condo, or multi-unit building, find the posted evacuation route from your floor to the exit. Walk it once. Identify where you would meet other residents outside the building. If your building has a fire alarm or generator-backed elevator, ask the manager when they last tested.
